title: My family — possession
title_target: Đây là gia đình của tôi.
goal: Name family members with the right words, express possession with *của* — and see that *của* can be dropped, just as English often skips "of".
bekal: express possession with *của*, and know when it can be dropped
name family members, which are distinguished by age and by the father's or mother's side
ask and answer about jobs with *làm nghề gì?*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ảnh gia đình
dialogs.intro: In the campus canteen. Budi shows a photo of his family to Nam, a married classmate.

lines.text: Ảnh này đẹp quá! Ai đây?

lines.text: Cháu ba tuổi. Cháu là con một.

notes: **Của means "of, belonging to", and it's often dropped.** *Gia đình **của** tôi* and *gia đình tôi* both mean "my family" (literally "family of me" / "family me"), and the short one is actually heard more. It's a bit like English choosing "my house" over "the house of mine".

**Vietnamese family words make more distinctions than English ones.** English "brother" and "sister" don't say who's older; Vietnamese always does — *anh* (older) vs *em* (younger) — and then adds male or female (*anh trai* / *chị gái*, *em trai* / *em gái*). For grandparents, uncles and aunts it also says whether they're on the father's or the mother's side.

**Cháu means "grandchild" and "niece/nephew" at once**, and is also a gentle way to refer to any small child — as Nam does with his own daughter in the last line. More importantly, *cháu* is the word you use for **yourself** when speaking to someone your grandparents' age.

**Chỉ … thôi wraps the sentence and means "only … just".** *Chỉ có ba người thôi* = "there are just three of us". *Chỉ* goes in front, *thôi* at the end; either can be dropped, but using both together sounds most natural in conversation.

**Làm nghề gì? is the standard way to ask about someone's job** — literally "do what profession?". Don't confuse it with *làm gì?*, "what are you doing (right now)?". *Anh làm nghề gì?* asks about a profession; *Anh làm gì đấy?* asks what you're busy with at the moment.

**Chị cả means "eldest sister"**, and birth order uses *thứ*: *chị thứ hai* (second sister), *em thứ ba* (third sibling). ⚠️ In southern Vietnam the count shifts by one: the eldest child is called *thứ hai*, not *thứ nhất*. If a southern family calls their first child "number two", that's why.

grammars.title: Của — possession, and when it disappears
body: The pattern is **thing + (của) + owner** — like English "the book of mine", never "my book" order. The thing owned comes first, the owner after.

Meaning
Can it be dropped?
rows: ✗ **required** — it's the point of the sentence
✗ **required** — it's the point of the sentence

after: ⚠️ **Của can't be dropped when it is itself the point of the sentence.** If the sentence is about whose something is, *của* must stay: *Cái này của tôi.* — not *Cái này tôi.* Just as English can't shorten "this is mine" to "this is me".
*Của ai?* = "whose?" and *của tôi* = "mine" are two ready-made chunks you'll need constantly — at a guesthouse, at the airport, at a shared table.

grammars.title: Family: one word for each place
body: There's no single word that just means "brother" or "sibling", and no general "uncle". You have to know **older or younger**, and for the generation above, **the father's or the mother's side**.
after: ⚠️ **Nội means "inside" and ngoại means "outside"** — the father's side was considered inside, the mother's side outside. By today's standards that's not very fair, but the words are frozen in the language and everyone uses them without thinking about where they came from.

The good news: most words in this table **are also used as pronouns** for strangers, just as some English speakers call older people "auntie" or "grandpa". So you're not learning two lists; you're deepening the same list from Unit 1.

blocks.text: Notice that many Vietnamese job names combine two words that each have their own meaning: *nông dân* = farming + people, *công nhân* = work + person, *đầu bếp* = head + kitchen. Taking them apart like this makes new words stick far better than memorizing the sound as a whole.
To answer, just *Tôi là* + job: *Tôi là kỹ sư.* If you don't work yet: *Tôi còn đi học.* ("I'm still in school") or *Tôi chưa đi làm.* ("I don't work yet").

head: Question
Say it
Meaning
rows: Gia đình anh có mấy người?
Za dìng ang kó mấy người?
How many people are in your family?
What do you do (for a living)?
Anh có mấy anh chị em?

blocks.title: One answer that saves a lot of conversations
items: *Anh có gia đình chưa?* will be asked of you again and again, and simply answering *Chưa* is enough and polite. Adding *Chưa, em còn đi học ạ.* ("Not yet, I'm still a student") closes off follow-up questions in a friendly way.

⚠️ Notice that the question uses *chưa* ("not yet"), not *không* ("no") — Vietnamese treats having a family as only a matter of time. Answering with *không* sounds like rejecting the idea altogether, which comes across much harsher than you intend.
There are five people in my family.
My older sister is a nurse.
